       1             SENATOR BONACIC:  Good morning.

       2             My name is John Bonacic, and I chair

       3      Senate Judiciary.

       4             I'm joined by Senator Ruth Hassle-Thompson,

       5      who's my ranker, by Senator Dilan, Senator Breslin.

       6             We're here today to discuss whether or not

       7      the maintenance provisions, with respect to the

       8      no-fault divorce, should be revisited.

       9             To many, it may not sound like a glitzy

      10      subject, but for many people who have the pain of

      11      going through a divorce, this subject is extremely

      12      important.

      13             Our first witness is the Law Revision

      14      Commission, but before I call them up, I'd like to

      15      welcome everyone to this public hearing.

      16             Before I start, I'd like to share with you

      17      some background.

      18             In 2010, what is commonly known as the

      19      "no-fault divorce" was signed into law in

      20      New York State.

      21             As many of you know, New York was the last

      22      state to pass a no-fault divorce.

      23             The state's Law Revision Commission was also

      24      asked to submit a comprehensive report to the

      25      Legislature on the state of spousal-maintenance





 

                                                                  4
       1      awards, both temporary awards, which are typically

       2      in place during the pendency of a divorce, and final

       3      maintenance awards for the period of time after the

       4      divorce becomes final.

       5             In May of this year, the

       6      Law Revision Commission submitted their completed

       7      report based on three years of data and input from

       8      various organizations affected by spousal

       9      maintenance, and matrimonial-law experts, from

      10      across the state.

      11             Today we'll hear testimony from members of

      12      the Law Revision Commission who submitted the

      13      report.

      14             We'll also be hearing from organizations that

      15      are interested in the subject matter of this report.

      16             We'll discuss, among other things, the

      17      existing standards for maintenance, the proposed

      18      changes, the nature of judicial discretion for

      19      higher-income earners, whether there should be

      20      differing standards of fault based on divorce cases,

      21      or whether the nature of judicial discretion

      22      effectively addresses that.

      23             I know it may not be in your prepared

      24      remarks, but I read a "Law Journal" article a week

      25      or two ago about the volume of no-fault divorces





 

                                                                  5
       1      being determined in New York County, specifically

       2      Manhattan.

       3             I know that a judge in Manhattan is proposing

       4      different standards for venue in no-fault cases, and

       5      would be interested in hearing comments on that.

       6             My hope is that, based on the oral and

       7      written testimony that is provided to this

       8      Judiciary Committee, we can formulate a legislative

       9      response to the issues surrounding maintenance

      10      award.

      11             At this time, I'd like to invite

      12      Senator Thompson to make any comments that she would

      13      like to make.

      14             Senator.

      15             SENATOR HASSELL-THOMPSON:  Thank you.

      16             You've never given me an open invitation to

      17      make any comments I wanted before.

      18                  [Laughter.]

      19             SENATOR HASSELL-THOMPSON:  Thank you,

      20      Chairman Bonacic.

      21             And I want to thank you again for your

      22      support in 2010 for the very same maintenance

      23      statutes under review today, and for the historic

      24      passage of no-fault divorce in New York State.

      25             I think it is safe to say, that without your





 

                                                                  6
       1      support, this would not have happened.

       2             Also, a great supporter of needed changes in

       3      our domestic-relations and family court law is

       4      Mr. Peter Kiernan, now chair of the

       5      Law Revision Commission, and in the past, counsel to

       6      Governor Paterson; and as such, a lawyer well

       7      acquainted with the laws we will talk about today.

       8             I join Chairman Bonacic in thanking all of

       9      the commission members and staff.

      10             Matrimonial litigation is a prolonged,

      11      expensive, and painful experience for tens of

      12      thousands of New Yorkers.

      13             As noted in the commission's report, in 2009,

      14      the most recent year for which records are available

      15      in New York, 50,310 marriages ended in dissolution,

      16      49,816 through a divorce proceeding.

      17             Maintenance in a fundamental bone of

      18      contention in many divorces.

      19             In prior public hearings, we learned that

      20      across New York, there were no consistent

      21      applications of the law governing maintenance

      22      awards.

      23             We also learned that the law was so

      24      subjective, that it was impossible for either party

      25      to predict what would happen.





 

                                                                  7
       1             This unpredictability was believed to be the

       2      cause of increased litigation and costly legal

       3      bills; and, so, we created a formula that prompted

       4      consistency and predictability for most litigants,

       5      and if it could also reduce the cost of litigation,

       6      we would be very pleased.

       7             In 2010, we also directed the State Law

       8      Review Commission to look at the practical effects

       9      of the new law, and to report to us about how the

      10      law is working, or not working; whether there's

      11      anything we can do to make the laws even better.

      12             I look forward to hearing from the

      13      commission, and other leaders, about our maintenance

      14      laws, and, thank you.

      15             SENATOR BONACIC:  Thank you, Ruth.

      16             We're joined by Senator Betty Little.

      17             The other three Senators that are here are

      18      reserving their comments; they're here to listen.

      19             And we're going to start with

      20      Witness Number 1, which is, Rosemary Bailly, the

      21      executive director of the New York State

      22      Law Revision Commission, with Peter Kiernan, the

      23      chair of that commission.

      24             So we would ask you to come up and share your

      25      thoughts with us.





 

                                                                  8
       1             ROSEMARY BAILLY, ESQ.:  Good morning.

       2             SENATOR BONACIC:  Hi, Rosemary.  Good

       3      morning.

       4             Peter, good morning.

       5             PETER KIERNAN, ESQ.:  Mr. Chairman, members

       6      of the Committee, I'm Peter Kiernan.  I'm Chair of

       7      the Law Revision Commission.

       8             And thank you for inviting us to testify on

       9      our report that was issued in May of this year, as

      10      indicated, as was requested and directed by the

      11      Legislature.

      12             I'm accompanied by Rosemary Bailly, who is

      13      the executive director of the commission.

      14             In 2010, as part of the no-fault-divorce

      15      legislation, the commission was directed by the

      16      Legislature to study maintenance laws, and to make

      17      recommendations that would alleviate the problems of

      18      inconsistency, unpredictability, of maintenance

      19      awards; and, particularly, with respect to temporary

      20      awards in pending divorce cases.

      21             Inconsistency and unpredictability reduce the

      22      likelihood of settlement;

      23             They increase the cost of obtaining a

      24      divorce;

      25             They make a divorce proceeding, especially





 

                                                                  9
       1      for low-income families, very burdensome;

       2             They strain the court system, which, as

       3      Senator Thompson indicated, has over 50,000 divorce

       4      actions annually.

       5             Now, we found in our review that these valued

       6      objectives were only partially achieved.

       7             So today, with your indulgence, I would like

       8      to discuss, just very briefly, the big ideas, the

       9      big themes, in the 2010 legislation, and in our

      10      report of this year.

      11             Rosemary will discuss matters of very

      12      important detail.

      13             The biggest idea, other than "no fault," in

      14      the 2010 package, was the adoption of a formulaic

      15      approach to determining awards.

      16             And as part of that package, 236(B) of the

      17      Domestic Relations Law was amended.

      18             They had a new section, that provided an

      19      award of temporary maintenance would be based on the

      20      application of a formula to the income of the

      21      parties.

      22             And that was up to $500,000 of the income of

      23      the spouse with the higher income.

      24             Now, this formulaic approach was an enormous

      25      departure from prior law.





 

                                                                  10
       1             When the 2010 legislative no-fault-divorce

       2      package was promulgated, as was mentioned, I was

       3      serving as counsel to the Governor.

       4             Parenthetically, I had no idea at the time

       5      that I was going to be appointed as Chair of the

       6      Law Revision Commission.

       7             That was a goodbye gift that

       8      Governor Paterson gave me on the way out the door.

       9             But, as counsel, I was very aware of the

      10      lobbying campaign that accompanied the legislation.

      11             Now, the fundamental advocacy was for spousal

      12      justice.  Primarily, that was advocacy for women's

      13      rights.

      14             And there was no resistance to that goal, and

      15      there was virtually no opposition to the

      16      legislation, at least when it got to the Governor's

      17      desk.

      18             Many thought that a formulaic approach could

      19      achieve the goals of the legislation, but since a

      20      formula was such a huge departure from prior law, it

      21      was wise of them, in my judgment, for the

      22      Legislature to ask the Law Revision Commission to

      23      review the implementation of this new law.

      24             And after a thorough analysis, a data-driven

      25      analysis; a non-ideological, non-partisan analysis,





 

                                                                  11
       1      which Ms. Bailly will describe, we found that, up to

       2      a certain level of income, the formulaic approach to

       3      determine temporary-maintenance awards works very,

       4      very well.

       5             In circumstances where there is little

       6      marital income, not many marital assets, the formula

       7      tends to produce quick decisions and awards, uses

       8      court time very efficiently, keeps costs low, and

       9      leads to rapid settlements of the entire underlying

      10      divorce proceeding, but more importantly, it leads

      11      to just results, and the empowerment of spouses,

      12      usually women, who theretofore did not have

      13      bargaining leverage, or the means to access judicial

      14      relief; and, thus, were denied even the opportunity

      15      for justice.

      16             Now, whether the underlying issue was spousal

      17      abuse, spousal domination, or spousal fear, the

      18      surety that an impartial formula would be applied

      19      quickly and inexpensively encouraged those who,

      20      otherwise, would have forsaken their rights to

      21      proceed and get relief.

      22             Of this, there is no doubt, and we salute the

      23      advocates of such spouses who, coincidentally, also

      24      were the advocates -- primary advocates for the

      25      legislation.





 

                                                                  12
       1             But the commission also found, that as the

       2      level of marital income increased, and assets of the

       3      marriage became greater and more varied, a formula

       4      actually begins to lose effectiveness, and it

       5      actually becomes counterproductive.

       6             While greater income levels suggest there may

       7      be equal access to lawyers, higher-education levels,

       8      and enhanced bargaining leverage for both parties,

       9      the more important fact is, that when assets are

      10      complex, involving houses, investment vehicles, a

      11      melange of debt inequity, often accompanied with tax

      12      structuring and estate considerations --

      13      estate-planning considerations, a two-dimensional

      14      formula simply is not apt.

      15             Equally significant, domestic-relations

      16      professionals and judges that we consulted with very

      17      broadly, advised us that an inept formula makes

      18      efficient settlements less likely and makes

      19      litigation more likely.

      20             Experienced professionals, experienced

      21      judges, know how to settle complex financial

      22      matters, and they should be encouraged to do so

      23      without artificial restraint.

      24             Now, we concluded that an income cap of up to

      25      $500,000, below which the formula would apply, and





 

                                                                  13
       1      above which it would not, was neither realistic nor

       2      helpful.

       3             Based on data, we recommend, and recommended,

       4      that the formula cap -- formula income cap be set at

       5      the same level as the Child Safety [sic] Standards

       6      Act, which level is indexed to the Consumer Price

       7      Index and adjusted biannually.

       8             If that were the case, there would be a

       9      consistent formula for ascertaining both

      10      child support and temporary maintenance, rather than

      11      two different formulas being applied to the same

      12      assets of the same family.

      13             There also would be less forum shopping.

      14             There would be no difference in the

      15      application of the formula from the family court,

      16      the civil court, the county court, or the

      17      Supreme Court, and there were differences prior to

      18      the legislation.

      19             The objectives of consistency and

      20      predictability, along with efficiency, would be

      21      served.

      22             Now, the data indicates, that we reviewed,

      23      that about 78 percent of all joint-income tax filers

      24      in New York State make less than the current

      25      Child Safety [sic] Standards Act income cap, which,





 

                                                                  14
       1      today, is $136,000.

       2             Accordingly, more than 75 percent of

       3      taxpayers would remain subject to the formula.

       4             And that would be consistent with the

       5      Legislature's objective, when it announced, and

       6      adopted, the Child Safety [sic] Standards Act.

       7             The announced objective was, that it would

       8      apply to the vast majority of New Yorkers.

       9             That would be achieved.

      10             Now, the commission also -- incidentally,

      11      just with respect to data, there was some advocacy

      12      that the cap be reduced to $200,000.

      13             More than 95 percent of all taxpayers make

      14      less than $200,000.

      15             But we settled on a hundred and thirty-six,

      16      because it was, as I said, 77, 78 percent, but the

      17      level of complexity begins to very much change once

      18      you get to the higher level.

      19             The commission also applied the same

      20      data-driven, non-ideological, non-partisan,

      21      commonsensible approach to other issues, such as

      22      duration-of-marriage factors, and whether judges

      23      should be mandated to write elaborate explanations

      24      whenever they decided to deviate from a formulaic

      25      guideline.





 

                                                                  15
       1             I think, Senator, you mentioned in your

       2      opening remark about some of the judges' reactions.

       3             On the latter -- on that point, on the latter

       4      point, we think judges should be judges, because we

       5      saw evidence that if judges were forced to explain

       6      in writing their every deviation from a formulaic

       7      guideline, many would be inclined not to deviate, in

       8      order just to avoid what they consider to be a

       9      non-essential task, even though justice may require

      10      that there be deviation.

      11             Members of the Committee, the Legislature

      12      made an important step when it embraced no-fault

      13      divorce.

      14             In doing so, it shed centuries of

      15      arbitrariness and artificiality.

      16             Courts are not the best place to sort out the

      17      tangled, and sometimes tortured emotions, of human

      18      nature, and of a marriage.

      19             Formulas also can be artificial and

      20      arbitrary, especially when the facts to which they

      21      are applied are not linear; when numerical values

      22      are a function of time frames, judgment, events, and

      23      interconnections.

      24             Emphatically, formulas are not driven by

      25      ideology, and should not be applied to serve





 

                                                                  16
       1      ideology.

       2             I'm going to yield to Rosemary, who's going

       3      to cover some other points.

       4             I'd be delighted to answer any questions you

       5      may have about our approach, our report, our

       6      findings.

       7             SENATOR BONACIC:  I would suggest that

       8      Rosemary finish her testimony, and then we can

       9      direct our questions to either one of you.

      10             Thank you, Peter.

      11             PETER KIERNAN, ESQ.:  Mr. Chairman, thank

      12      you.

      13             And, Senators, thank you for inviting me to

      14      appear with Peter today.

      15             As Peter mentioned in his presentation, the

      16      legislative package included a formula for the

      17      determination of temporary maintenance.

      18             And you may recall, actually, at that time,

      19      the legislation had a formula for permanent

      20      maintenance, but then there was some readjustments

      21      that appeared in the temporary maintenance.

      22             So the law, as it was passed in 2010, didn't

      23      make any changes to maintenance awards in final --

      24      at a final determination of the divorce.

      25             So as a consequence, we right now in New York





 

                                                                  17
       1      have two different approaches to maintenance:

       2             In a temporary maintenance, we have a

       3      formulaic approach designed to achieve consistency

       4      and predictability;

       5             And in the post-divorce maintenance, we have

       6      a more nuanced approach, where a judge can look at a

       7      set of factors and mold the determination based on

       8      what it can glean from the particular case.

       9             So the scope of our work included whether

      10      to -- to consider whether to adopt a formula for

      11      post-divorce awards.

      12             And as Peter noted, the information that

      13      we've gather seemed to indicate that both approaches

      14      have merits, depending on the amount of assets and

      15      the amount of income involved.

      16             So what I want to just talk a little bit

      17      about today is the work that the commission did that

      18      led to its report.

      19             It had basically three aspects:

      20             The research, case law, and statutes in other

      21      jurisdictions;

      22             The collection, review, and analysis of both

      23      statistical data gathered by the State Department of

      24      Taxation and Finance, the census bureau in the

      25      nine counties that we actually looked at;





 

                                                                  18
       1             And our own data that we attempted to collect

       2      through the cooperation of the Office of Court

       3      Administration.

       4             And since this is the Judiciary Committee,

       5      I feel it's important to note, we had extremely good

       6      cooperation with the Office of Court Administration

       7      on a task that took a number of years.

       8             So I really appreciate, very much, their

       9      efforts.

      10             And we noted that in our report.

      11             We also did a lot of outreach, both,

      12      formally, informally, with judges around the state,

      13      various practitioners who practice -- whose clients

      14      are wealthy, who have middle-class clients, and who

      15      have lower-income clients.

      16             And I see a number of those individuals that

      17      we had contact with present here today.

      18             At the time we were considering our study, a

      19      number of states had either -- either a number of

      20      states or a number of counties within states had

      21      adopted a formulaic approach to maintenance.

      22             There were very few that were statutorily

      23      enacted, but, it was clear from the literature that

      24      the movement was towards formulas, although, as I'm

      25      sure that you'll hear, a lot of people had some





 

                                                                  19
       1      objections to formulas, in general.

       2             What the formulas all had in common, though,

       3      whether they were adopted formally or informally,

       4      was that they were developed by attorneys with

       5      expertise in the nature and frequency of maintenance

       6      awards in the jurisdiction, who used anecdotal

       7      evidence and reported decisions to craft formulas,

       8      including income caps, which would merit a range of

       9      results they presumed would have an appropriate

      10      starting point for negotiations for their clients.

      11             And we actually talked to people in those

      12      areas, jurisdictions, and where there were reports,

      13      we read them as well, to understand how they came

      14      about.

      15             So, to the extent that they were based on

      16      their own jurisdictions, they provided little in the

      17      way of guidance, in terms of how we should approach

      18      it; although, we saw the idea of a formula as having

      19      some merit.

      20             As part of our study, we collected, reviewed,

      21      and analyzed data from over 7,000 divorce

      22      proceedings in 9 counties across the state.

      23             They were Albany, the Bronx, Erie, Jefferson,

      24      Kings, Nassau, and New York, Onondaga, and

      25      Westchester.





 

                                                                  20
       1             And I should say that, my colleague at the

       2      time, Barbara Hancock, who has since retired, she

       3      and I actually read every single questionnaire, and

       4      it was informative, although, of limited value.

       5             I mentioned that we had done this work with

       6      the Office of Court Administration.

       7             Because of the amount of information that we

       8      were getting, but the lack of its completeness, we

       9      were delayed in completing our report, because we

      10      hoped to gather as much information as possible that

      11      we could bring to bear on our conclusions.

      12             We hoped to learn about the relationship

      13      between any awards and the length of marriage, the

      14      health of the parties, their respective incomes, and

      15      the presence of unemancipated children.

      16             And we also hoped to learn if there were any

      17      differences between the amounts of awards, prior to,

      18      and after, the enactment of the

      19      temporary-maintenance formula.

      20             And we had the assistance of a senior dean

      21      and a professor of economics from Syracuse Maxwell

      22      School in helping us to analyze this data.

      23             Now, despite the large number of

      24      questionnaires that we collected, and our thorough

      25      review of the data, both, statistically analysis, as





 

                                                                  21
       1      well as, actually, hands-on review of the

       2      questionnaires, the paucity of information provided

       3      in these questionnaires made it difficult to draw

       4      any statistically significant conclusions, but we

       5      were able to report several things:

       6             One, the awards appeared to be likely when

       7      there were unemancipated children, the husband's

       8      income was higher than that of his spouse, his

       9      health was good, and the marriage was a lengthy one.

      10             If a formula, like a temper [ph.] maintenance

      11      formula, were used to calculate a final maintenance

      12      award, 56 percent of the cases reporting no award,

      13      where they reported income, would have benefited

      14      from the [unintelligible] of a formula.

      15             The responses that we saw from reading the

      16      questionnaires revealed a pattern of low income,

      17      service-industry jobs, and information that was

      18      consistent with the statistical data from those

      19      counties.

      20             Over the course of our study, while we were

      21      gathering all this data, we also, with our

      22      commissioners together, and individually, and our

      23      staff, then, two attorneys, conducted formal and

      24      informal outreach to bar associations, judges, and

      25      practitioners.





 

                                                                  22
       1             I've mentioned a few that we spoke with:

       2      representatives from the American Academy of

       3      Matrimonial Lawyers, the family-law section of the

       4      New York State Bar, the Post-Marital Income

       5      Coalition, the Women's Bar Association of the

       6      State of New York, and other practitioners

       7      representing parties with incomes of varying

       8      amounts.

       9             We also received written submissions from a

      10      number of people, including the number that I just

      11      mentioned, as well as the Suffolk County Bar

      12      Association, the New York Legal Assistance Group,

      13      and the Lawyers Committee Against Domestic Violence.

      14             In October 2011, we hosted a roundtable

      15      discussion at Albany Law School, where we heard from

      16      various stakeholders, many of whom I have mentioned,

      17      and they discussed maintenance awards, the problems

      18      and concerns about the interpretation of the

      19      temporary-maintenance statute, as well as the

      20      post-divorce-maintenance statute, and suggestions

      21      for change.

      22             And as a conclusion, there appeared to be a

      23      consensus on the broad outlines of the approach that

      24      we were suggesting; namely, the application of a

      25      formula on an income up to a certain level, and then





 

                                                                  23
       1      the application of statutory factors on income in

       2      excess of that cap, or where the application of the

       3      formula would lead to inappropriate results.

       4             The commission's recommendations are detailed

       5      in our report, as well as more information on the

       6      data, that's contained in the appendices, but

       7      I would like to conclude with just a few remarks on

       8      the three aspects of the report:

       9             The duration of the post-divorce-maintenance

      10      awards, assuming that you have -- however you're

      11      going to make that determination, how long should

      12      the party receive the maintenance?

      13             The increased earning capacity as a marital

      14      asset, as a result of the O'Brien decision;

      15             And Section 412 of the Family Court Act.

      16             The duration of an award of post-divorce

      17      maintenance, we looked at various sources to try to

      18      determine how to approach that.
